accounts.bio: Self-described self-care educator for people whose problems aren't being solved by conventional medicine. A certified health coach and herbalist who runs Grimm's Apothecary in Port Jervis, NY, which sells herbal tonics, blue lotus and magnesium chloride. His posts focus on magnesium and other minerals, circadian light (sunrise, avoiding artificial blue light), digestion, herbal pharmacology and neurochemistry. He sometimes disagrees with the pro-metabolic crowd: he has called the 'seed oils cause obesity via the endocannabinoid system' argument flawed, and an older weight-loss thread of his recommended high-protein / high-fat eating with complex carbs only.
accounts.circle_note: This is the account the site started from. He is part of the loose 'BowTied' network of X accounts. His threads quote Ray-Peat-themed accounts such as @peatpill and @bioenergy_space, which puts him in the same conversation as the accounts below.
accounts.commercial_note: He sells products (magnesium chloride, herbal tonics) and runs a paid Patreon. Some posts link to supplement brands.
accounts.limits: Logged out, X shows only about 6 of his recent posts. Everything else here comes from Thread Reader App archives (mostly 2021–2025), the X embed (syndication) endpoint for single posts whose IDs we already knew, his website and one podcast.

accounts.name: Master Metabolism
accounts.followers_note: Follower counts on third-party mirrors don't agree (one says ~9K, another ~41K), so none is given here.
accounts.bio: Runs the 'Master Metabolism' Substack and X account, and describes himself as a writer and researcher on metabolism, health and vitality. Most of his writing is about hypothyroidism and low T3: he argues that TSH and T4 tests miss problems at the cell level, prefers NDT or T3 over T4-only treatment, and points to body temperature as a guide. He also writes about near-infrared light for Hashimoto's, selenium, serotonin, seed oils and calcium. Some of his framing comes straight from Ray Peat (for example a thread titled 'CO2 and Cancer – Ray Peat'). He sells a paid hypothyroidism video course and uses affiliate links with a discount code for light devices.
accounts.verification: There are two similar names. 'Master Metabolic' (mastermetabolic.com, @mastermetabolic) is a Utah coaching company and is NOT this account. 'Master Metabolism' was confirmed as @lowmegatron three ways: (1) X's own embed endpoint returns posts by screen_name 'lowmegatron' with display name 'Master Metabolism' (e.g. status 2068801190867902593, 21 Jun 2026); (2) the Substack at lowmegatron.substack.com is titled 'Master Metabolism'; (3) Rattibha's author page lists 'Master Metabolism @lowmegatron' with the same bio and the thyroid course link.
accounts.circle_note: He works in the same Ray Peat / bioenergetic framework as the accounts below (anti-PUFA, anti-serotonin, pro-thyroid, pro-sugar). We did not find a public source showing him appearing with the Bioenergetic View hosts, so that link is shared ideas, not a documented collaboration.
accounts.commercial_note: Sells a hypothyroidism course and posts affiliate links with a discount code for near-infrared devices.
accounts.limits: His Substack is public. Logged out, his X timeline and replies can't be read. Only a handful of posts were checked through X's embed endpoint and thread mirrors.

accounts.name: Jay Feldman
accounts.person: Jay Feldman, host of The Energy Balance Podcast
accounts.bio: Wellness coach, writer and host of The Energy Balance Podcast. His blog argues that health 'comes down to energy' and that sugar doesn't cause diabetes or inflammation. He also argues that low-carb, fasting and 'eat less, exercise more' raise stress hormones, that omega-3 fish oils aren't the 'healthy fats', that most people don't need to restrict salt, that drinking more water isn't better, and that T4-only thyroid medication and TSH tests mislead.
accounts.circle_note: He co-hosts the 'Bioenergetic View' podcast series with Danny Roddy and Mike Fave, and Georgi Dinkov has been a guest (BV #3, Oct 2024).
accounts.limits: Neither his site nor search results gave a verifiable X handle, so no X link is shown. Claims come from his blog and podcast pages.

accounts.name: Mike Fave
accounts.bio: Coach whose tagline is 'I help you rebuild your metabolism, to revive your health.' On the Bioenergetic View podcast he argues that relying on fat oxidation (as on low-carb diets) causes 'reductive stress' in the mitochondria. He also argues that hormetic stressors such as fasting, heat or fish oil work by causing damage first, and that blood hormone levels can hide what's happening inside tissues.
accounts.circle_note: Co-host of the Bioenergetic View with Jay Feldman and Danny Roddy (Ray Peat Forums thread, Sep 2024).
accounts.verification: The X handle @MikeFaveScience was matched on a third-party X viewer, where the bio is identical to the tagline on mikefave.com.
accounts.limits: His site is a single landing page. The claims here come from his own statements in the BV #3 transcript.

accounts.name: Danny Roddy

links.label: Article: 4 misconceptions about the bioenergetic view of pattern hair loss

accounts.bio: Long-time popularizer of Ray Peat's ideas, best known for a 'bioenergetic' explanation of pattern hair loss. He argues it comes from low energy metabolism, stress hormones and inflammation, not genes and DHT alone. He tracks thyroid function with resting pulse and underarm temperature, recommends calcium, vitamin D and K2, and has published 'Lost Conversations with Ray Peat'.
accounts.circle_note: Co-host of the Bioenergetic View with Jay Feldman and Mike Fave, and long-time collaborator of Georgi Dinkov on the Generative Energy podcast.
accounts.verification: The handle @dannyroddy is the title of his own link page (dannyroddy.com). His X profile couldn't be opened without a login.
accounts.limits: Claims come from his Substack. His Patreon coaching content is paywalled and wasn't used.

accounts.name: Georgi Dinkov (Haidut)
accounts.person: Georgi Dinkov, runs IdeaLabs and the haidut.me blog
accounts.bio: Best-known disciple of Ray Peat online. He blogs at haidut.me and sells supplements through IdeaLabs. His recurring themes are that estrogen and serotonin are harmful 'stress' substances, that burning glucose beats burning fat, that chronic fasting promotes cancer, and that niacinamide, vitamin K and aspirin are protective.
accounts.circle_note: A frequent guest of Danny Roddy (Generative Energy) and of the Bioenergetic View hosts (BV #3, Oct 2024).
accounts.verification: Third-party X viewers list @haidut as 'Georgi D.', with links to haidut.me.
accounts.limits: Claims come from his own words in the BV #3 transcript. His X timeline couldn't be read logged out.

accounts.name: Ray Peat (foundational source)
accounts.bio: Biologist and newsletter writer whose essays are the source of most 'pro-metabolic' ideas: thyroid and CO2 as protective, sugar and saturated fat as good fuels, and polyunsaturated oils, estrogen and serotonin as harmful. He also wrote that salt restriction is harmful and that coffee is nutritious. He didn't use X, but every other account here either quotes him or works in his framework.
accounts.circle_note: Cited by name in Master Metabolism's threads and in the Bioenergetic View podcast. Danny Roddy publishes 'Lost Conversations with Ray Peat'.
accounts.limits: Only the public raypeat.com articles were used.

accounts.bio: An X account posting nutrition and supplement advice, mostly as replies. Its recurring themes are high-dose vitamin B1 (thiamine), vitamin K2 for arterial plaque, vitamin C for thyroid autoimmunity, magnesium, boron and taurine, along with strong scepticism of statins and mainstream medicine. It says it gives guidance to clients. No website was found.

Other look-alike handles (@Betel_juice, @Beteljuice_) didn't look health-related. Web searches for 'Betel Juice' mostly return an Indian craft beer.
accounts.circle_note: It overlaps with the thiamine / magnesium side of this circle and replies to accounts like @EO_Nutrition and @Helios_Movement. It's less Peat-focused than the other accounts.
accounts.commercial_note: No product or shop was found. Posts mention helping 'clients'.
accounts.limits: Read through X's public API (about 40 recent posts). Most posts are short replies, so the claims are short too.

accounts.name: FixLowBodyTemp.com
accounts.followers_note: A website, not an X account.
accounts.bio: Steve Richfield, who describes his background as computers, electronics and adaptive control systems, says the body's 'central metabolic control system' (CMCS) in the hypothalamus can learn faults the way a self-tuning HVAC controller does. His aim is to restore a 98.6°F / 37°C daytime temperature through guided, deliberate physiological stress. He says plainly that he has no medical credentials and works for donations.
accounts.circle_note: He shares this circle's focus on low body temperature (the Broda Barnes / Peat tradition) but explains it with control theory, not with thyroid or diet.
accounts.commercial_note: Asks for donations in exchange for the encryption key to the full version of his book. A free stripped-down version is offered.
accounts.limits: Only the home page could be read. The /papers/ library returned 403 and the box's certificate check failed, so the book and questionnaire weren't reviewed.

claims.claim: The heart weighs only about 0.3 kg and burns roughly 100–130 kcal a day at rest, rising only modestly during hard exercise. This was posted in support of the quoted point that muscle isn't a big calorie furnace either.
claims.quote: "The human adult male heart only weighs ~0.3kg, burning a modest 100–130 calories/day at rest"
claims.evidence_note: Organ-level measurements give the heart about 440 kcal/kg/day, so roughly 130–145 kcal/day for a 0.3 kg heart. That's close to his figure, perhaps slightly low. Skeletal muscle burns about 13 kcal/kg/day at rest, which supports the quoted point that adding muscle raises resting burn only modestly.

evidence_refs.label: Wang et al. 2010, Am J Clin Nutr – specific metabolic rates of organs (heart ≈440 kcal/kg/day, muscle ≈13 kcal/kg/day)

claims.claim: Rather than cutting salt alone, raise potassium and magnesium relative to sodium, aiming for roughly twice as much potassium as sodium in the diet.
claims.evidence_note: Good evidence that a lower sodium-to-potassium ratio goes with lower blood pressure, and that more potassium lowers blood pressure. A specific 2:1 target isn't an established guideline. People with kidney disease or on some blood-pressure drugs need to be careful with potassium.

evidence_refs.label: 2021 Adv Nutr meta-analysis: urinary sodium-to-potassium ratio and blood pressure
Aburto et al. 2013, BMJ – increased potassium intake lowers blood pressure

claims.claim: Magnesium is foundational for the nervous system. Deficiency may be common, and different magnesium forms feel different depending on the person, so form and dose should be individualized.
claims.evidence_note: Magnesium is essential, and trials for anxiety and sleep often report some benefit, but they are small and inconsistent. One open-label trial reported improvement in depression. Higher magnesium intake modestly lowers blood pressure, mainly in people with hypertension or low magnesium. Head-to-head evidence that particular forms work better for mood is thin.

evidence_refs.label: 2024 systematic review: magnesium for anxiety and sleep (positive but small, heterogeneous trials)
Tarleton et al. 2017, PLoS One – open-label RCT of magnesium for depression
2025 Hypertension meta-analysis of 38 RCTs: magnesium and blood pressure

claims.claim: Start with sunrise: getting outdoor light at dawn is the most important and easiest light habit, ahead of other interventions.
claims.quote: "At least start with the sunrise. That's gonna be the most important and probably the easiest"
claims.evidence_note: Timed light exposure, especially morning light, reliably shifts the body clock and affects melatonin timing. Effects on mood and sleep in healthy people are less consistent.

evidence_refs.label: 2019 systematic review: light exposure and human circadian rhythm

claims.claim: Artificial blue light is harmful at any time of day, and worst after sunset. He recommends incandescent bulbs, turning off artificial light after dark and wearing blue-light blockers indoors.
claims.source_label: Threads (Jan 2022; Apr 2024), via Thread Reader App
claims.evidence_note: Evening room light clearly suppresses and delays melatonin. But reviews of blue-blocking glasses find mixed or no clear benefit for sleep, and there is no good evidence that daytime indoor light is 'toxic'.

evidence_refs.label: Gooley et al. 2011, JCEM – room light before bed suppresses melatonin
2021 systematic review: blue-blocking glasses for sleep and mood (mixed)
2023 Cochrane review: blue-light filtering lenses – no clear sleep benefit

claims.claim: Melatonin is mostly made inside mitochondria in response to daytime infrared light, so calling it only the 'hormone of darkness' is outdated.
claims.evidence_note: This comes from a hypothesis advanced mainly by one research group (Reiter and colleagues). Mitochondria can make melatonin, but the idea that sunlight's near-infrared drives meaningful melatonin production in human tissues hasn't been shown in human studies. The night-time pineal melatonin rhythm is well established.

evidence_refs.label: 2023 review (Reiter group): melatonin and near-infrared radiation – hypothesis

claims.claim: Artificial blue light, irregular sun exposure and non-native EMF are a bigger factor in skin cancer and melanoma than the sun itself.
claims.evidence_note: This goes against the evidence. Solar UV radiation is classified by IARC as a Group 1 human carcinogen and is the main environmental cause of skin cancers, including melanoma. No comparable evidence links indoor blue light or EMF to melanoma.

evidence_refs.label: IARC 2009, Lancet Oncol – solar UV radiation is a Group 1 human carcinogen

claims.claim: Tasting bitter foods and herbs on the tongue (not swallowing capsules) helps keep stomach-acid and digestive-enzyme production up through bitter receptors and the vagus nerve.
claims.evidence_note: Bitter-taste receptors exist in the stomach as well as the tongue, and one study found caffeine raises gastric acid through them. Good human trials showing that tasting bitters improves digestion are lacking.

evidence_refs.label: Liszt et al. 2017, PNAS – caffeine triggers gastric acid via bitter-taste receptors in parietal cells

claims.claim: The popular 'seed oils / linoleic acid cause obesity by acting like cannabis on CB1 receptors' theory is flawed. It also contradicts the parallel claim that linoleic acid causes depression.
claims.evidence_note: Mouse studies do show high-linoleic diets raise endocannabinoids and weight gain. In humans, higher linoleic-acid levels in the blood are linked to lower, not higher, cardiovascular risk, although one recovered trial found no mortality benefit from swapping in LA-rich oil. Overall the human evidence is mixed. This post is notable because it pushes back on a core pro-metabolic idea.

evidence_refs.label: Alvheim et al. 2012, Obesity – linoleic acid raises endocannabinoids and obesity in mice
Marklund et al. 2019, Circulation – higher linoleic acid biomarkers linked to lower CVD and mortality
Ramsden et al. 2016, BMJ – Minnesota Coronary Experiment re-analysis (no mortality benefit of LA-rich diet)

claims.claim: Nattokinase at about 10,800 FU a day was reported to improve atherosclerosis and blood lipids. He cautions that it isn't replicated and may interact with blood thinners or BP medication.
claims.evidence_note: His caution is justified. The study he cites was open-label, without a placebo. A randomized placebo-controlled trial found nattokinase did NOT slow atherosclerosis progression. Bleeding risk with anticoagulants is a real concern.

evidence_refs.label: Chen et al. 2022, Front Cardiovasc Med – open-label nattokinase study (1,062 participants)
Hodis et al. 2021 – randomized placebo-controlled trial: nattokinase had no effect on atherosclerosis progression

claims.claim: For copper problems, support zinc, magnesium, molybdenum, boron, B vitamins and sunlight. He argues serum zinc-to-copper should be about 1:1, and that a 1:2 ratio means much higher disease risk.
claims.evidence_note: Some observational studies link a higher copper-to-zinc ratio to worse outcomes in older adults. A 1:1 'optimal' serum ratio and the multi-supplement protocol haven't been tested in trials. Excess zinc can itself cause copper deficiency.

evidence_refs.label: 2025 Exp Gerontol cohort: copper-to-zinc ratio and mortality in older ED patients (observational)

claims.claim: Common antibiotics (e.g. ciprofloxacin, doxycycline, metronidazole) can wipe out Oxalobacter formigenes, a gut bacterium that breaks down oxalate.
claims.evidence_note: Studies show antibiotic courses can lastingly reduce O. formigenes colonization, and colonization is linked to fewer calcium-oxalate kidney stones. His specific drug list wasn't checked one by one.

evidence_refs.label: Kharlamb et al. 2011, J Endourol – antibiotics reduce Oxalobacter formigenes colonization
Kaufman et al. 2008, JASN – O. formigenes colonization linked to lower stone risk

claims.claim: Magnesium chloride (in baths, foot soaks, diluted topically or orally) is his preferred form. He sells a high-purity version and argues the chloride helps magnesium enter cells.
claims.evidence_note: Oral magnesium chloride is absorbed reasonably well. But there is little good evidence that magnesium is meaningfully absorbed through the skin from baths or sprays, and the cell-entry mechanism isn't established. Note that this is a product he sells.

evidence_refs.label: Gröber et al. 2017, Nutrients – 'Myth or Reality: Transdermal Magnesium?'

claims.claim: For healthy weight loss he proposed a strict framework: lots of sun, high-protein / high-fat eating with only complex carbs, daily (preferably raw) seafood, game meat instead of beef, heavy lifting, cold exposure, blood donation and 'magnesium saturation'.
claims.evidence_note: This is a mix of many unrelated steps, so it can't be assessed as one claim. Raw seafood carries food-safety risks. This older advice differs from the pro-sugar stance of the Ray-Peat-style accounts on this site.

claims.claim: Overcoming chronic social isolation (he moved across the country to be near close friends) did more for his mental health than any biohacking.
claims.evidence_note: Strong evidence from large meta-analyses that social connection is linked to better health and survival, on a scale comparable to well-known risk factors.

evidence_refs.label: Holt-Lunstad et al. 2010, PLoS Med – social relationships and mortality meta-analysis

claims.claim: TSH is an unreliable guide to whether cells are getting enough active thyroid hormone (T3). Stress, overtraining, calorie or carb restriction and fasting can lower TSH and hide 'low T3' states.
claims.evidence_note: Partly right. Illness and calorie restriction do lower T3 without raising TSH, which is well documented. But TSH remains a well-validated test for primary hypothyroidism, the most common kind, and whether low T3 during stress should be treated is debated.

evidence_refs.label: Fliers et al. 2015, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol – thyroid function in critical illness (low T3, TSH not raised)
Fontana et al. 2006, JCEM – long-term calorie restriction lowers T3
ATA 2014 guidelines for treating hypothyroidism (levothyroxine first-line)

claims.claim: Stress raises energy demand beyond supply, which slows metabolism through thyroid changes (more reverse T3, less T3) that standard blood tests often miss: 'hidden hypothyroidism'.
claims.evidence_note: The low-T3 / high-reverse-T3 pattern in severe illness and starvation is real ('non-thyroidal illness'). Most endocrinologists see it as an adaptation rather than a disease to treat, and evidence for treating it in everyday stress is lacking.

evidence_refs.label: Fliers et al. 2015, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol – thyroid function in critical illness (low T3, TSH not raised)
Fontana et al. 2006, JCEM – long-term calorie restriction lowers T3

claims.claim: T4-only treatment (levothyroxine) often leaves people with symptoms. Dosing with T3 or NDT to optimize the T3 : reverse-T3 ratio produced large symptom improvements in one clinical series.
claims.evidence_note: Some patients stay symptomatic on levothyroxine. Guidelines now allow a trial of T4 + T3 in selected patients, but randomized trials mostly show no average benefit over T4 alone. The series he cites was uncontrolled.

evidence_refs.label: ATA/BTA/ETA 2021 consensus on LT4/LT3 combination therapy
ATA 2014 guidelines for treating hypothyroidism (levothyroxine first-line)

claims.claim: 24-hour urinary free T3 may be the closest thing to an objective test of thyroid hormone sufficiency. It tracks symptoms better than blood T4 or TSH and stays low on levothyroxine.
claims.evidence_note: This rests mainly on work from one clinical group. We found no large independent validation, and urinary free T3 isn't used in mainstream guidelines.

evidence_refs.label: ATA 2014 guidelines for treating hypothyroidism (levothyroxine first-line)

claims.claim: Body temperature (and the old basal-metabolic-rate test) is a key indicator of T3 activity in cells and should be part of judging thyroid status.
claims.evidence_note: It's well established that thyroid hormone drives heat production (thermogenesis). We found no modern validation of home body temperature as a reliable diagnostic test, because many other factors affect it.

evidence_refs.label: Mullur et al. 2014, Physiol Rev – thyroid hormone regulation of metabolism and thermogenesis

claims.claim: Near-infrared light (e.g. 830 nm on the thyroid) may be the most effective Hashimoto's treatment. In a pilot study, 47% of patients no longer needed thyroid medication.
claims.evidence_note: The pilot (15 patients, no control group) and a follow-up placebo-controlled trial (43 patients) both came from the same Brazilian group, and a small 2026 trial reported symptom improvement. Promising but small and not independently replicated. Note: the post includes affiliate links for light devices.

evidence_refs.label: Höfling et al. 2010 – low-level laser therapy pilot in autoimmune thyroiditis (n=15, no control group)
Höfling et al. 2013 – randomized placebo-controlled LLLT trial (n=43, same group)
2026 Lasers Med Sci – photobiomodulation for fatigue/behaviour in Hashimoto's (small trial)

claims.claim: New research shows near-infrared light reduces anxiety, depression, fatigue, pain and sleep problems in Hashimoto's patients within 3 weeks, even while they stay on levothyroxine.
claims.quote: "near infrared light crushes anxiety, depression, fatigue, pain, and sleep problems in Hashimoto's"
claims.evidence_note: A small 2026 trial reported symptom improvements in both groups, with some between-group differences favouring active light. That's one small study, so treat 'crushes' as overstatement.

evidence_refs.label: 2026 Lasers Med Sci – photobiomodulation for fatigue/behaviour in Hashimoto's (small trial)

claims.claim: Selenium (e.g. 200 mcg/day) is needed to convert thyroid hormone and calms autoimmune thyroid disease. In one trial it lowered TPO antibodies about three times more than placebo.
claims.evidence_note: A 2024 meta-analysis found selenium lowers TSH and TPO antibodies in Hashimoto's. An earlier Cochrane review judged the evidence low quality, and lower antibodies don't clearly translate into better symptoms. Too much selenium is toxic.

evidence_refs.label: Gärtner et al. 2002, JCEM – selenium lowers TPO antibodies
2024 Thyroid meta-analysis (35 studies): selenium lowers TSH, TPOAb in Hashimoto's without hormone therapy
Cochrane 2013: evidence for selenium in Hashimoto's incomplete / low quality

claims.claim: Serotonin is not a 'happy hormone'. It lowers metabolic rate and body temperature, promotes fat storage and is elevated in type 2 diabetes and obesity.
claims.source_label: Substack: 'How Serotonin Made You Fat, Cold, and Diabetic' (Sep 2025)
claims.evidence_note: There's some support: blocking peripheral (gut-made) serotonin increased brown-fat heat production and protected mice from obesity. An umbrella review found no consistent evidence that low serotonin causes depression. But that doesn't show serotonin causes anxiety or depression either, and brain and gut serotonin act differently.

evidence_refs.label: Crane et al. 2015, Nat Med – blocking peripheral serotonin synthesis raises brown-fat thermogenesis (mice)
Moncrieff et al. 2023 umbrella review – no consistent evidence that low serotonin causes depression

claims.claim: Ginger acts as a natural anti-serotonin agent, raises heat production, helps weight loss and eases low-thyroid symptoms.
claims.evidence_note: Meta-analyses show ginger modestly lowers body weight and some metabolic markers, and one 2022 RCT looked at ginger for persistent hypothyroid symptoms. The anti-serotonin mechanism comes mostly from animal and lab studies.

evidence_refs.label: 2019 meta-analysis: ginger modestly lowers body weight and some metabolic markers
2022 RCT: ginger for persistent symptoms in controlled hypothyroidism

claims.claim: Seed oils (PUFA, mainly linoleic acid) increase 'feed efficiency' and suppress resting metabolic rate. That's why livestock fatten on them, and it may contribute to human obesity.
claims.evidence_note: The argument relies mainly on animal feeding studies. Controlled human studies don't consistently show PUFA lowers metabolic rate, and higher linoleic-acid levels are linked to lower cardiovascular risk in people.

evidence_refs.label: Alvheim et al. 2012, Obesity – linoleic acid raises endocannabinoids and obesity in mice
Marklund et al. 2019, Circulation – higher linoleic acid biomarkers linked to lower CVD and mortality

claims.claim: Linoleic acid from seed oils 'feeds' cancer. In rodents, diets with linoleic acid produced much larger tumours.
claims.evidence_note: Rodent tumour studies do show this. Large human cohort data on linoleic-acid biomarkers show no rise, and if anything a slight fall, in cancer and overall mortality. Animal findings haven't carried over to humans.

evidence_refs.label: Marklund et al. 2019, Circulation – higher linoleic acid biomarkers linked to lower CVD and mortality
Ramsden et al. 2016, BMJ – Minnesota Coronary Experiment re-analysis (no mortality benefit of LA-rich diet)

claims.claim: Prevent harmful calcification by eating plenty of calcium (preferably dairy), keeping the calcium-to-phosphate ratio at least 1:1, getting vitamin D and K2, and keeping PUFA and serotonin low.
claims.evidence_note: High phosphate is linked to cardiovascular disease, and vitamin K2 improved arterial stiffness in one RCT. The PUFA and serotonin parts are speculative, and calcium supplements (unlike food) have been debated for heart risk.

evidence_refs.label: Dhingra et al. 2007, Arch Intern Med – higher serum phosphorus linked to CVD (observational)
Knapen et al. 2015 RCT – MK-7 (vitamin K2) improved arterial stiffness

claims.claim: Thyroid hormone itself raises ferritin regardless of iron stores. So low ferritin may partly reflect low thyroid activity rather than only low iron.
claims.source_label: Substack: 'The Influence of Thyroid Hormone on Ferritin' (Sep 2026)
claims.evidence_note: Lab work shows thyroid hormone affects the iron-regulatory proteins that control ferritin production, and ferritin shifts with thyroid status. A plausible mechanism, but what it means for diagnosing iron deficiency in practice isn't well studied.

evidence_refs.label: Leedman et al. 1996, J Biol Chem – thyroid hormone modulates iron-regulatory proteins and ferritin mRNA

claims.claim: High cortisol causally raises the risk of obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, insomnia, depression, fatty liver, low T3 and high blood pressure. He gives tips to keep it down.
claims.evidence_note: Pathologically high cortisol (Cushing's syndrome) clearly causes most of these problems. Whether everyday variation in cortisol causes them is much less certain. We didn't find a specific source to verify the word 'causally' for normal-range cortisol.

claims.claim: Quoting Ray Peat: baking soda helps tumours mainly by supplying carbon dioxide, an idea he traces back to 18th-century experiments.
claims.source_label: X thread 'CO2 and Cancer – Ray Peat' (Dec 2024)
claims.evidence_note: Mouse studies show bicarbonate can raise tumour pH and reduce metastases. There's no clinical evidence that baking soda treats cancer in people, and large doses are dangerous.

evidence_refs.label: Robey et al. 2009, Cancer Res – bicarbonate raises tumour pH, reduces metastases in mice

claims.claim: Sodium bicarbonate reduces lactic acid and improves muscle performance, which researchers have linked to higher natural-birth rates when labour stalls.
claims.evidence_note: Bicarbonate as an exercise aid is well supported. We didn't verify the labour / C-section study in this check.

evidence_refs.label: ISSN 2021 position stand: sodium bicarbonate and exercise performance

claims.claim: Sugar does NOT cause insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes. He argues fat and stress hormones are the real drivers.
claims.source_label: Blog: 'Sugar Does NOT Cause Insulin Resistance or Diabetes' (2018)
claims.evidence_note: The evidence goes against this as a blanket statement. Sugar-sweetened drinks consistently raise diabetes risk. Whole fruit is linked to lower risk, so the source and form of sugar matter.

evidence_refs.label: Malik et al. 2010, Diabetes Care – sugar-sweetened beverages raise type 2 diabetes risk
Muraki et al. 2013, BMJ – whole fruit linked to lower diabetes risk; fruit juice to higher

claims.claim: Low-carb diets and 'becoming a fat burner' push the body into a stress state and are a poor strategy for health and fat loss.
claims.source_label: Blog: 'Why NOT to be a Fat Burner' (2017)
claims.evidence_note: Long-term calorie and carbohydrate restriction can lower T3. But many trials show low-carb diets work about as well as others for weight loss and blood sugar, at least in the short term. The evidence is mixed rather than clearly harmful.

evidence_refs.label: Fontana et al. 2006, JCEM – long-term calorie restriction lowers T3
de Cabo & Mattson 2019, NEJM – review of intermittent fasting benefits

claims.claim: Omega-3s (fish oil) are not the 'healthy fats'. As highly unsaturated fats they oxidize easily and he argues they do more harm than good.
claims.evidence_note: The Cochrane review found omega-3 supplements have little or no effect on overall mortality, so the hype is overstated. That doesn't show they are harmful, and this check didn't assess possible harms.

evidence_refs.label: Cochrane 2020 – omega-3s have little or no effect on all-cause mortality

claims.claim: Most people shouldn't restrict salt. Low-salt diets raise stress hormones and the research doesn't support blanket restriction.
claims.evidence_note: Salt reduction reliably lowers blood pressure, especially in people with hypertension. But very low sodium does raise renin and aldosterone and blood lipids a little, so the evidence on outcomes is debated, more so for people with normal blood pressure.

evidence_refs.label: He et al. 2013, BMJ/Cochrane – modest salt reduction lowers blood pressure
Graudal et al. 2020 Cochrane – low vs high sodium: BP falls, but renin/aldosterone/lipids rise

claims.claim: Drinking more water is not better. Drinking past thirst dilutes electrolytes and may stress the body.
claims.evidence_note: Healthy adults have no scientific basis for the '8 glasses a day' rule, and drinking to thirst is usually enough. Severe over-drinking can cause dangerously low sodium.

evidence_refs.label: Valtin 2002 – no scientific basis for '8 × 8' water advice in healthy adults

claims.claim: T4-only thyroid medications often make hypothyroid people feel worse, and TSH tests are a poor guide to thyroid status.
claims.source_label: Blog: 'Why T4-only Medications Often Make Hypothyroidism Worse…' (2017)
claims.evidence_note: Some patients stay symptomatic on T4 and guidelines allow trying T3 in some of them. But trials show no average benefit of combination therapy, and TSH remains the standard test for primary hypothyroidism.

evidence_refs.label: ATA/BTA/ETA 2021 consensus on LT4/LT3 combination therapy
ATA 2014 guidelines for treating hypothyroidism (levothyroxine first-line)

claims.claim: 'What doesn't kill you makes you stronger' is misapplied: fasting, ketogenic diets and calorie restriction are sold as healthy hormesis but work by stressing the body.
claims.evidence_note: This is a contrarian view. Many reviews report metabolic benefits of intermittent fasting, though long-term human outcome data are limited and calorie restriction does lower T3.

evidence_refs.label: de Cabo & Mattson 2019, NEJM – review of intermittent fasting benefits
Fontana et al. 2006, JCEM – long-term calorie restriction lowers T3

claims.claim: Relying mainly on fat for fuel (low-carb, fasting) over-reduces the mitochondria ('reductive stress', low NAD+/NADH). Burning carbohydrate well is the better way to keep NAD+ high.
claims.evidence_note: This is a mechanistic argument drawn from cell biology (the Randle cycle, electron-transport-chain biochemistry). It hasn't been tested as a diet recommendation in human trials.

evidence_refs.label: 2023 Nutrients review of NAD+ precursors (mostly preclinical)

claims.claim: Hormetic tools (fasting, heat stress, fish oil's oxidized fats) 'induce dysfunction first' to trigger protective responses, and these stresses add up over time.
claims.evidence_note: This is a philosophical stance more than a testable claim. Human data on fasting and other hormetic practices show some benefits, and long-term harms haven't been shown.

evidence_refs.label: de Cabo & Mattson 2019, NEJM – review of intermittent fasting benefits
Cochrane 2020 – omega-3s have little or no effect on all-cause mortality

claims.claim: Blood hormone levels can be misleading. Tissues convert hormones locally (cortisol, estrogens, T4 to T3), so normal serum values can hide what's happening in cells.
claims.evidence_note: Local hormone conversion inside tissues is well documented, for example thyroid hormone activation. That serum tests are therefore unreliable for diagnosis doesn't follow automatically.

evidence_refs.label: Mullur et al. 2014, Physiol Rev – thyroid hormone regulation of metabolism and thermogenesis

claims.claim: Pattern hair loss is better explained by low energy metabolism, stress hormones and inflammation (a 'bioenergetic' view) than by genes and DHT alone.
claims.source_label: Substack: '4 Common Misconceptions About The Bioenergetic View of Pattern Hair Loss' (2021)
claims.evidence_note: He cites real studies linking hair loss with thyroid problems, cortisol, inflammation and lipid oxidation, but these are associations. DHT-blocking drugs such as finasteride regrow hair in trials, which undercuts the 'genes and DHT are inadequate' claim, even if those drugs have side effects.

evidence_refs.label: 2022 network meta-analysis of hair-regrowth treatments in androgenetic alopecia (finasteride, minoxidil, etc.)

claims.claim: Track resting pulse and underarm temperature on waking and in the afternoon (Broda Barnes style) as practical proxies for thyroid function and metabolic stress, along with TSH, prolactin, PTH, vitamin D and reverse T3.
claims.evidence_note: Thyroid hormone does influence heat production and heart rate. But home temperature and pulse haven't been validated as diagnostic tests, and the lab panel he lists isn't a standard thyroid workup.

evidence_refs.label: Mullur et al. 2014, Physiol Rev – thyroid hormone regulation of metabolism and thermogenesis

claims.claim: More dietary calcium plus vitamins D and K2 can lower PTH and prolactin, and may help hair in younger people.
claims.evidence_note: Adequate calcium and vitamin D do lower PTH. Evidence that this reverses pattern hair loss is lacking.

evidence_refs.label: Knapen et al. 2015 RCT – MK-7 (vitamin K2) improved arterial stiffness

claims.claim: Replace hard-to-digest grains, beans and vegetables with ripe sweet fruit and juices, and use Ray Peat's raw carrot salad for bowel problems.
claims.evidence_note: Whole fruit is linked to lower diabetes risk, but fruit juice to higher risk. We found no studies of the carrot salad, and replacing grains, beans and vegetables with juice hasn't been tested.

evidence_refs.label: Muraki et al. 2013, BMJ – whole fruit linked to lower diabetes risk; fruit juice to higher

claims.claim: Estrogen is a known human carcinogen, and even low-dose, long-term estrogen therapy is risky. Menopause is not truly an estrogen-deficiency state.
claims.evidence_note: IARC does classify estrogen-progestogen therapy as carcinogenic, and the WHI combined-therapy arm raised breast-cancer risk. But in the WHI estrogen-alone arm, breast cancer incidence and deaths were LOWER, and the 'not deficient' claim goes against standard endocrinology.

evidence_refs.label: IARC Monograph 91 – combined estrogen-progestogen therapy is carcinogenic to humans
WHI 2002, JAMA – estrogen plus progestin raised breast cancer and CVD risk
Chlebowski et al. 2020, JAMA – estrogen-alone arm had LOWER breast cancer incidence and mortality

claims.claim: Serotonin is a 'misery/stress hormone'. It lowers metabolism, drives fibrosis and fatty liver, and anti-serotonin drugs act as antidepressants.
claims.evidence_note: Peripheral serotonin is involved in metabolic disease in animal studies, and the 'low serotonin causes depression' theory is weakly supported. But SSRIs beat placebo modestly in trials, and the blanket claim that serotonin is harmful isn't established.

evidence_refs.label: Crane et al. 2015, Nat Med – blocking peripheral serotonin synthesis raises brown-fat thermogenesis (mice)
Moncrieff et al. 2023 umbrella review – no consistent evidence that low serotonin causes depression
Cipriani et al. 2018, Lancet – all 21 antidepressants (incl. SSRIs) beat placebo, modest effect

claims.claim: Chronic fasting and constant AMPK activation promote cancer and diabetes. Don't restrict sugar for cancer, because fat oxidation is the bigger problem.
claims.evidence_note: This goes against current reviews, which on balance report metabolic benefits from intermittent fasting. Human evidence that fasting causes cancer is lacking. The anecdotes given (e.g. Steve Jobs) aren't evidence.

evidence_refs.label: de Cabo & Mattson 2019, NEJM – review of intermittent fasting benefits

claims.claim: Niacinamide is the best NAD+ precursor because it also inhibits CD38 and PARP. Combine it with something that re-oxidizes NADH, such as vitamin K, methylene blue or certain antibiotics.
claims.evidence_note: Comparisons of NAD+ precursors are mostly preclinical. Methylene blue can cause serotonin syndrome when combined with serotonergic drugs, and taking antibiotics as a 'supplement' is not advisable.

evidence_refs.label: 2023 Nutrients review of NAD+ precursors (mostly preclinical)
2018 systematic review: methylene blue-induced serotonin syndrome

claims.claim: Salt restriction (especially combined with diuretics) is harmful, notably in pregnancy. Adequate salt supports energy and metabolic rate.
claims.source_label: raypeat.com: 'Salt, energy, metabolic rate, and longevity'
claims.evidence_note: Salt reduction lowers blood pressure in trials. Very low sodium raises renin and aldosterone, and outcome data at the low end are debated. Routine salt restriction in pregnancy isn't recommended today.

evidence_refs.label: He et al. 2013, BMJ/Cochrane – modest salt reduction lowers blood pressure
Graudal et al. 2020 Cochrane – low vs high sodium: BP falls, but renin/aldosterone/lipids rise

claims.claim: TSH can't be read on its own. Interpret thyroid status using body temperature, pulse, the Achilles-reflex relaxation time and blood markers such as cholesterol, albumin, glucose, sodium and lactate.
claims.source_label: raypeat.com: 'TSH, temperature, pulse rate, and other indicators in hypothyroidism'
claims.evidence_note: Some of these signs, like a slow Achilles reflex and high cholesterol, are recognized clinical features of hypothyroidism. None replaces TSH and free T4 for diagnosis in current guidelines.

evidence_refs.label: ATA 2014 guidelines for treating hypothyroidism (levothyroxine first-line)
Mullur et al. 2014, Physiol Rev – thyroid hormone regulation of metabolism and thermogenesis

claims.claim: Eating sugar doesn't cause diabetes. Diabetes is a problem of stress and fat metabolism, and sugar (glucose / sucrose) can even be protective.
claims.evidence_note: Sugar-sweetened beverages consistently raise type 2 diabetes risk. Whole fruit is linked to lower risk. Fatty acids do contribute to insulin resistance, so part of the mechanism is right, but the overall claim goes against the epidemiology.

evidence_refs.label: Malik et al. 2010, Diabetes Care – sugar-sweetened beverages raise type 2 diabetes risk
Muraki et al. 2013, BMJ – whole fruit linked to lower diabetes risk; fruit juice to higher

claims.claim: Polyunsaturated oils (seed and fish oils) suppress thyroid function and promote degeneration. Saturated fats such as coconut oil are safer.
claims.evidence_note: Animal data support some of the mechanisms. In human cohorts, higher linoleic acid is linked to lower cardiovascular risk. The Minnesota Coronary Experiment re-analysis is a notable exception (no mortality benefit).

evidence_refs.label: Marklund et al. 2019, Circulation – higher linoleic acid biomarkers linked to lower CVD and mortality
Ramsden et al. 2016, BMJ – Minnesota Coronary Experiment re-analysis (no mortality benefit of LA-rich diet)

claims.claim: Coffee is a nutritious 'vitamin-like' food that supports thyroid, liver and metabolism rather than a harmful drug.
claims.source_label: raypeat.com: 'Caffeine: A vitamin-like nutrient, or adaptogen'
claims.evidence_note: Large umbrella reviews link moderate coffee drinking with lower mortality and lower liver-disease risk (observational). Pregnancy and poor sleep are exceptions. The 'vitamin-like' framing is his own.

evidence_refs.label: Poole et al. 2017, BMJ – umbrella review: coffee generally associated with benefit

claims.claim: 'Sundowning' confusion in older people is mainly a thiamine (B1) shortage. Food isn't enough, so everyone should take about 500 mg of B1 every morning.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: People with SIBO are usually very low in B1 and should take around 500 mg of thiamine each morning.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: Calcium plaque in arteries and kidney stones mostly comes from too little vitamin K2 (MK-7), not from cholesterol. Statins are pushed by drug-industry messaging.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: People with Graves' or Hashimoto's often need 2–4 g of vitamin C a day. Raise the dose until your stool loosens; if it doesn't change, you aren't taking enough.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: Tinnitus can come from an overactive stress (sympathetic) response driven by glutamate. Magnesium, high-dose B1 and taurine help calm it.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: Thiamine is needed to clear excess glutamate, so a B1 shortage can lock in a cycle of stress.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: Steady boron (plus biotin) helps fight candida. Americans get about half the boron they need (~1.5 mg vs ~3 mg a day), so supplementing makes sense.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: High cortisol drives Graves' disease and Hashimoto's, so lowering cortisol is a priority.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: A daily morning dose of benfotiamine, the fat-soluble form of B1 (~300 mg), is his baseline recommendation.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: Daytime body temperature that stays below 98.6°F / 37°C is a fault in a learned 'central metabolic control system' in the hypothalamus. It's often mistaken for hypothyroidism or 'Wilson's syndrome'.
claims.evidence_note: There's no published evidence for this 'CMCS' model. The idea of a fixed 37°C 'normal' is itself disputed: large datasets put average oral temperature closer to 36.6°C and show it varies between people.

claims.claim: These control faults are about learning ('computation'), not chemistry, so drugs can't truly fix them. The system has to be reprogrammed through outside influences.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: The control system can learn a fault from 'superstitious' events such as general anaesthesia, years of comfortable sedentary life, a past illness like hypothyroidism, famine, or even the mother's condition in the womb.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: The fix is to deliberately apply carefully planned physiological stresses (heat, cold, exertion and the like) that push the system to reset for good. It's unpleasant and shouldn't be done alone.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: The protocol has five stages: diagnosis (e.g. checking temperature during a hot shower), learning to estimate your own temperature, an initial reset (often in one day), stabilisation, and about a year of recovery.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: Low body temperature leads to 'hypothyroid' symptoms and, he claims, clogged arteries, cancer and autoimmune disease. A temperature stuck at 37°C causes insomnia, and being unable to enter ketosis causes obesity.
claims.evidence_note: These causal links come from his own case experience. We found no clinical studies behind them.

claims.claim: Around 37°C the body regulates temperature smoothly (proportional / PID-like). At lower temperatures it switches systems on and off, which is why people with low temperatures often have hands that are either hot or cold.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: Long-term keto keeps stress hormones (adrenaline, noradrenaline, cortisol, glucagon) higher than a diet with more than about 150 g of carbs a day does, and this harms metabolism.
claims.source_label: Substack: 'How The Ketogenic Diet Slows Your Metabolism'
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: For men, about 8–14% body fat is best for T3. More fat raises estrogen and lowers T3, but getting extremely lean slows the body down too.
claims.source_label: Substack: 'How to Create Natural T3 Optimization Plan'
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: Lifting weights 3–4 times a week and eating enough food support T3. Overtraining and long or harsh calorie cuts suppress it.
claims.source_label: Substack: 'How to Create Natural T3 Optimization Plan'
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: Copper matters for T3 as much as zinc does. Many people get less than the 0.9 mg/day RDA (he suggests about 2.6 mg is optimal), and too much zinc can cause a copper shortage.
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: Capsaicin from chili peppers is one of the few fat-burner supplements with real research behind it: it curbs appetite and raises metabolic rate and fat burning.
claims.source_label: Substack: '7 Fat Burner Supplements that Raise Metabolic Rate'
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: Sunlight is the best source of vitamin D, so supplements are for winter or indoor periods. Aim for at least 35 ng/ml, and get enough vitamin A because the two work together.
claims.source_label: Substack: 'How to change your life with Vitamin D'
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.

claims.claim: DHT is the stronger and more useful androgen, not the cause of hair loss, and some foods can raise it naturally.
claims.source_label: Substack: '9 Foods to Boost DHT Levels'
claims.evidence_note: Not yet checked against the research literature.
